title: Can Agents Use a Computer Yet? We've Got the Data | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z argues computer-use agents crossed from demo to production in early 2026 — best OSWorld-Verified score jumped from 42% to 85% versus ~72% for humans — but the model layer is now commoditized and the durable advantage sits in harness design, verification, and company-specific workflow context. At roughly $6-8/hour of inference, agents are break-even against ~$10/hour offshore BPO and imply 70-80% gross margins against $30-45/hour US back-office labor, so the binding constraint is no longer cost or capability but which tasks have machine-observable ground truth.

insights.claim: On the OSWorld-Verified desktop-agent benchmark, the best computer-using model scored 42% a year ago (early 2025) and 85% today, versus the ~72% that human testers score on the same tasks.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: The capability gate on back-office automation is already open; underwrite deployment risk, not model risk.
insights.quote: A year ago the best computer-using model scored 42% on OSWorld-Verified; today’s best scores 85%, above the ~72% humans manage on the same tasks
insights.locator: From Humans Watching Every Step to Real Autonomous Workflows

insights.claim: Claude Fable 5 is cited as the current computer-use leader at 85% on OSWorld-Verified, with scores drawn from the llm-stats.com leaderboard as of June 2026.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Frontier computer-use leadership is a moving target with rapid rank turnover — do not price a durable model moat.
insights.quote: Claude Fable 5, the current leader at 85%, is highlighted in gold
insights.locator: The benchmark chart tracks computer-use performance

insights.claim: A founder building in the space dates production-viability of computer-use models to a specific model release: they weren't good enough to deploy on their own until Opus 4.6 in February 2026.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Deployment cohorts and revenue ramps in this category should be dated from early 2026, not 2024 — TAM capture is only months old.
insights.quote: the models weren’t good enough to use in production on their own until Opus 4.6 in February 2026
insights.locator: And the capability jump is what made those setups viable

insights.claim: Gemini 3.5 Flash is excluded from the computer-use comparison because it has no native computer-use feature, making its reported score an internal research eval rather than a true agentic run.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Cross-lab computer-use score comparisons are frequently apples-to-oranges; verify whether a score came from a native agentic loop.
insights.quote: Gemini 3.5 Flash is left off because it has no native computer-use feature
insights.locator: All scores come from the llm-stats.com leaderboard

insights.claim: Almost nobody deploys consumer chat products for computer-use work; founders and enterprises build on the raw model APIs or buy from vendors who package them.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Consumer agent-mode usage is a poor proxy for enterprise computer-use demand; track API and vendor revenue instead.
insights.quote: almost nobody deploys consumer products (Claude, ChatGPT agent mode) for this
insights.locator: Notably, almost nobody deploys consumer products

insights.claim: Benchmark scores are a weak proxy for deployment viability because a business process only finishes if every step does, so an 85% task-completion rate still means 15 of 100 runs failed.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Model per-task accuracy compounds badly across multi-step processes — demand end-to-end process completion metrics from vendors.
insights.quote: OSWorld counts completed tasks, so 85% still means 15 of 100 failed, and a business process only finishes if every step does
insights.locator: Of course, benchmarks aren’t always the best proxy

insights.claim: Back-office automation only creates value if humans stop reviewing every output, because a process where a person reviews every result saves no labor — mirroring coding, where the scarce resource is no longer writing code but vouching for it.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Verification capacity, not generation capacity, is the binding constraint — bet on the verification and trust layer.
insights.quote: the scarce resource is no longer writing the code, it’s vouching for it
insights.locator: Back-office work doesn’t grade on a curve

insights.claim: An operator running millions of automated tasks a month could not say which model executes them, because his vendor swaps models underneath him the way a cloud provider swaps hardware.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Model choice is being abstracted into a substitutable input — the value accrues to the orchestration vendor, and model vendors face commodity pricing.
insights.quote: when your heaviest users stop checking the leaderboard, the leaderboard has stopped being the story
insights.locator: Perhaps the clearest tell is that one operator

insights.claim: Computer-using agents are strongest on standardized, repeatable, protocol-following tasks with a clear well-defined path, and break down on complex workflows where accuracy is harder to verify.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Screen deployments for task standardization and verifiability — those attributes, not industry, predict which automation vendors scale.
insights.quote: computer-using agents are strongest on standardized, repeatable tasks with a clear, well-defined path
insights.locator: Agents are Protocol Following

insights.claim: The real unlock for computer-use agents is the long tail of software where no clean API exists and a person would otherwise be clicking through a UI by hand, including government and insurance portals, regulatory pages, retail order processing, contract processing, and IT tickets in ServiceNow.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Legacy-software surface area with no API is the beachhead market — vendors serving API-less verticals have less competition from SaaS incumbents.
insights.quote: The real unlock is the long tail of software where no clean API exists
insights.locator: Agents are Protocol Following

insights.claim: A CPG data platform runs roughly 15-20 million automated portal interactions a month, using agents as a self-healing fallback for hand-coded scrapers that diagnoses a retailer portal UI change, fixes the automation, and keeps data flowing before an engineer sees the error.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Scraper-maintenance spend is an identifiable, budgeted cost pool being displaced now — a concrete near-term revenue wedge.
insights.quote: ~15-20M automated portal interactions a month, using agents as a self-healing fallback for hand-coded scrapers
insights.locator: a CPG data platform walked us through

insights.claim: After deploying agents as self-healing scraper fallbacks, one company cut the engineering team dedicated to scraper maintenance in half and re-allocated that staff capacity to other workflows.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: The first measurable ROI from computer-use is engineering headcount redeployment, not front-office headcount cuts — an easier internal sell and faster payback.
insights.quote: they cut the engineering team dedicated to scraper maintenance in half
insights.locator: Once implemented, they told us

insights.claim: A global systems integrator runs 27 live computer-use workflows processing roughly 1,500-2,100 IT tickets a day, with the explicit goal of redeploying 20-25% of headcount on low-margin managed-services contracts.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Labor-arbitrage IT services margins are the first P&L to re-rate; watch managed-services gross margin disclosures for the effect.
insights.quote: 27 live workflows leveraging computer use agents that process ~1,500-2,100 IT tickets a day
insights.locator: In another case, from a global systems integrator

insights.claim: An agency automated a recruiting workflow end-to-end into an applicant tracking platform using a cheap non-frontier model because it "does everything we need and does it well."
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Real workloads are already migrating down-market from frontier models — frontier token demand from this category may be smaller than assumed.
insights.quote: does everything we need and does it well
insights.locator: And finally an agency walked us through

insights.claim: The market for computer-use agents is still chipping away at low-hanging fruit — the authors encountered no sophisticated use cases among users they spoke with — though a long list of automatable workflows remains before harder tasks are needed.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Runway for simple, high-volume workflow automation is long; you don't need capability breakthroughs for the next several years of growth.
insights.quote: We did not encounter more sophisticated use cases among the users we spoke with, which tells us the market is still chipping away at the low-hanging fruit
insights.locator: We did not encounter more sophisticated use cases

insights.claim: The dominant failure pattern is not agents that cannot click, but workflows where there is no clear definition of what good looks like or no reliable way to determine whether a task succeeded.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Use output-verifiability as the primary diligence screen on any agentic automation vendor's target workflows.
insights.quote: there is either no clear answer for “what good looks like” (i.e. they are hard to evaluate) or no reliable way of determining whether a task succeeded
insights.locator: The clearest pattern is workflows where in theory

insights.claim: Silent data corruption is the key risk in un-cross-checkable extraction: an agent pulling payment terms from contracts into an ERP that reads "net 60" as "net 30" produces a record that looks plausible, passes every visual check, and is only caught when an invoice goes out wrong.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Plausible-but-wrong outputs create deferred financial liabilities — audit and reconciliation tooling is an adjacent investable need.
insights.quote: if it reads “net 60” as “net 30,” the record looks perfectly plausible, passes every visual check, and nobody catches it until an invoice goes out wrong
insights.locator: you can’t cross-check the output

insights.claim: Some workflows have no verification signal at the moment they run: an agent submits an insurance claim, the screen says "received," but two days later an adjuster phones about a policy number and the claim quietly stalls because the agent never learns the call happened.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Out-of-band ground truth (phone, mail, email) is the structural ceiling on autonomy in insurance and healthcare back office — a moat for whoever closes that loop.
insights.quote: the agent has no idea the call ever happened, and the claim quietly stalls
insights.locator: in some cases there is no signal to verify success at the time the task runs

insights.claim: A smarter model does not fix a process whose ground truth arrives as a phone call to somebody's desk a week later, unless the harness is designed to handle that edge case from the start.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Model-scaling optimism does not transfer to these workflows; the unlock is process instrumentation, so favor vendors doing workflow re-engineering.
insights.quote: a smarter model doesn’t fix a process whose ground truth shows up as a phone call to somebody’s desk a week later
insights.locator: Net-net is that a smarter model doesn’t fix a process

insights.claim: Designing for failure must be a first-class concern from the start, because a solution that handles failures poorly will never be adopted in production regardless of benchmark performance.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Failure-handling architecture is the real product diligence question — ask about escalation and retry design before model choice.
insights.quote: a solution that does not handle failures well will never be adopted in production
insights.locator: As a consequence, failure modes matter more than any benchmark

insights.claim: A recurring production pattern is run-caching: the agent executes a workflow once, the system caches it as deterministic code that runs cheaply thereafter, and the model only returns when something breaks — to diagnose, fix, and re-cache.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: This architecture makes revenue per workflow decline over its lifetime for usage-priced vendors while raising gross margin — a critical modeling input.
insights.quote: the agent runs the workflow once, the system caches it as deterministic code, runs execute as cheap repeatable code from then on, and the model comes back only when something breaks
insights.locator: One example of what this looks like in practice

insights.claim: Run-caching means cost per run falls over a workflow's lifetime and cheaper models simply lower the bill, while the agent absorbs the uncertainty that previously either broke deterministic code or required a human to review every failure.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Token consumption per automated workflow is deflationary over time — a headwind to inference-revenue extrapolations built on agent adoption.
insights.quote: cost per run falls over a workflow’s lifetime, and cheaper models just lower the bill
insights.locator: With this approach, cost per run falls

insights.claim: Enterprise buyers say the model itself is rarely the deciding factor because "the models today are already good enough"; they evaluate and pay for the infrastructure to run reliably at scale, pass security review, and prove ROI.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Pricing power is migrating from model layer to deployment layer; model-only differentiation stories in this category should be discounted.
insights.quote: the models today are already good enough
insights.locator: Buyers Care About Infrastructure

insights.claim: Buyers picked vendors on whether the product reported hours saved without extra work and whether a junior engineer could run it, making the moat being the vendor an enterprise is allowed and able to use at scale in production.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Built-in ROI reporting and low operator skill requirements are the concrete win/loss factors — score vendors on these, not demos.
insights.quote: the moat is not the frontier capability—rather, it’s being the vendor an enterprise is allowed, and able, to use at scale in production
insights.locator: They picked vendors on whether the product reported hours saved

themes.theme: Commoditization of Execution, Moat in Context

insights.claim: The execution layer of computer-use agents — Selenium, Playwright, Stagehand, and stitching together DOM or video recordings — is being abstracted away the same way Claude Code abstracted the scaffolding around coding agents, so clicking the right button is no longer a moat.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Browser-automation tooling startups face commoditization; the Claude Code precedent gives a template for who captures value at the scaffolding layer.
insights.quote: That whole execution layer is getting abstracted away, the same way Claude Code abstracted the scaffolding around coding agents
insights.locator: The Model Is Not the Differentiator, Context Is

insights.claim: The durable advantage is company-specific context — tribal knowledge, internal terminology, preferred formats, escalation paths, failure handling, and verification — which lives in runbooks, credentials, test cases, guardrails, and increasingly in a single recorded video of someone doing the job once.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Context capture is where switching costs and defensibility form; the video-of-the-job capture mechanism is a specific technique to watch as a wedge.
insights.quote: increasingly in a single recorded video of someone doing the job once
insights.locator: Unsurprisingly, the context and knowledge of the workflow are durable

insights.claim: Because workflow context is specific to a company and often to a single team, the next generation of agentic coworkers will be built at the application and context layer rather than the model layer, by focused startups rather than model providers.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Argues against model labs vertically capturing enterprise agent workflows — an argument for application-layer venture exposure.
insights.quote: the next generation of agentic coworkers gets built at the application and context layer, not the model layer
insights.locator: That said, it is exactly the kind of specific, unglamorous problem

insights.claim: Running a computer-use agent costs roughly $6-8 per hour of inference today, ranging $3-15 depending on screenshot frequency, context carried, and how much work is handed off to deterministic code.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: This is the reference price for agent-hours; harness design, not model list price, drives the spread.
insights.quote: Running an agent costs roughly $6-8 per hour of inference today, but in practice anywhere between $3 and $15
insights.locator: The cost data is also encouraging

insights.claim: A computer-use agent at ~$6-8/hour is roughly break-even against offshore India BPO labor at ~$10/hour fully loaded ($8-15 range, per 2026 rates from Globalify, HiveDesk, and 1840 & Co).
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Offshore BPO providers face no immediate cost advantage erosion but zero remaining cushion — their pricing floor is now set by inference curves.
insights.quote: an agent is roughly break-even against offshore BPO at ~$10/hour fully loaded
insights.locator: The Real Inflection is Economic, Not Just Technical

insights.claim: Against US back-office labor at $30-45/hour fully loaded — built up from the BLS median customer service rep wage of $20.59/hour plus benefits at ~30% of total comp and overhead — computer-use agents pencil out to a 70-80% gross margin.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: 70-80% gross margin against onshore labor is software-like economics for services work — the core case for agent-delivered BPO roll-ups.
insights.quote: pencils out to a 70-80% gross margin against US back-office labor at ~$30-45/hour
insights.locator: So read the comparison as the worst case

insights.claim: The quoted agent cost describes the most expensive mode — a frontier model operating the UI screenshot by screenshot — so well-built harnesses that reserve that mode only where needed see blended cost drop fast, meaning the published comparison is a worst case.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Real deployed economics are better than headline agent-hour pricing; the disclosed numbers understate the disruption to labor arbitrage.
insights.quote: These figures describe the agent operating the UI screenshot by screenshot with a frontier model – the most expensive mode there is
insights.locator: The cost data is also encouraging

insights.claim: In agentic mode, agents remain far slower than people — a task a person finishes in two to three minutes can take an agent eight to ten, with academic benchmarks showing an even wider gap — so the argument for agents is round-the-clock availability, fractional cost, and scaling without hiring, not speed.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite throughput gains from agent speed; the value is capacity elasticity and 24/7 coverage, which changes which workflows qualify.
insights.quote: a task someone finishes in two to three minutes can take an agent eight to ten
insights.locator: Same caveat on speed

insights.claim: The economics look different for vendors selling agent-hours than for BPO buyers: COGS are inference plus retries because failed runs still burn tokens, and margins compress when context grows or screenshot frequency rises.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Retry burn and context growth are the hidden margin killers in agent-services P&Ls — diligence gross margin at the workflow-variance level.
insights.quote: COGS are inference plus retries (i.e. failed runs still burn tokens) and margins compress when context grows or screenshot frequency goes up
insights.locator: This comparison works for BPO buyers and ops teams

insights.claim: There is no settled business model for selling agent labor: vendors price per task, per hour, or per outcome, each carrying a different risk profile depending on workflow variance, with monitoring, maintenance, and human escalation priced in as they would be for a human workforce.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Pricing-model choice is a signal of vendor confidence in workflow variance — outcome pricing implies verified reliability, per-task implies uncertainty.
insights.quote: There is no one-size-fits-all business model here yet, and the answer varies by vertical
insights.locator: Vendors manage this by pricing per task, per hour, or per outcome

insights.claim: The binding question is no longer whether the economics work but how far the set of reliably solvable tasks extends, because inference keeps getting cheaper and open-source models are getting good enough for a growing share of these workflows.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Reframes the investment question from cost to task coverage — track reliability expansion, not price per token, as the growth driver.
insights.quote: the real question is no longer whether the economics work – it’s how far the set of tasks that can be solved reliably extends
insights.locator: And the math only gets better

insights.claim: Labs and startups have poured hundreds of millions into computer-use RL environments — the sandboxes where models practice real tasks for reward — with Mechanize, Habitat, Fleet, Chakra, Deeptune, Matrices, and Originator building the training and eval substrate under the frontier models.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: A named private-market cohort supplying the training substrate — capability gains here were bought deliberately and will continue, so RL-environment vendors are a picks-and-shovels exposure.
insights.quote: companies like Mechanize, Habitat, Fleet, Chakra, Deeptune, Matrices, and Originator building the training and eval substrate underneath the frontier models
insights.locator: Where Do We Go From Here?

insights.claim: Most computer-use systems in production today are single-agent — one model, one task, one session — and multi-agent architectures with planners and parallel executors only start to matter as workflows get more complex and latency becomes a constraint, bringing memory, trust, and compounding failure-rate problems.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Multi-agent complexity is ahead, not present — dismiss vendor multi-agent marketing today, but watch for it as a leading indicator of workflow complexity.
insights.quote: Most computer-use systems deployed in production today are single-agent: one model, one task, one session
insights.locator: Architecture, though, is a different story

insights.claim: No standard orchestration framework exists for computer-use agents, so every interesting team is building bespoke orchestration — and the emergence of an abstraction layer, as happened for coding agents, is one of the more interesting unsolved infrastructure problems in the space.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: An explicitly flagged open infrastructure category with no incumbent — a direct green-field investment thesis.
insights.quote: that abstraction layer is one of the more interesting unsolved infrastructure problems in the space
insights.locator: The teams doing interesting work here are all building bespoke orchestration

insights.claim: Latency is the vector most likely to surprise people: some teams already cut it by grounding on the accessibility tree instead of screenshots, and Standard Intelligence's general computer action model trained on an 11-million-hour video dataset running at 30 FPS signals that the step-by-step screenshot loop is a solvable problem, not a permanent tax.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: If the screenshot loop is removed, agent cost and speed both improve step-function — a specific named company to watch as the trigger.
insights.quote: trained on an 11-million-hour video dataset, running at 30 FPS, and is an early signal that the step-by-step screenshot loop slowing today’s agents is a solvable problem, not a permanent tax
insights.locator: Latency is the one most likely to surprise people

insights.claim: Future progress runs along accuracy, latency, and cost, with accuracy most important as the difference between a demo and a solved problem, plus security and governance concerns including credentials, audit logs, data retention, prompt injection, permissioning, and accountability.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: Agent security and governance tooling — credentials, audit trails, prompt-injection defense — is an emerging adjacent spend category gated in front of enterprise scale.
insights.quote: These three vectors in addition to security and governance (e.g. credentials, audit logs, data retention, prompt injection, and accountability, permissioning)
insights.locator: From here, future developments run along three lines

insights.claim: The qualifying profile for enterprise computer-use today is narrow workflows with high volume, repetitive steps, stable business rules, legacy interfaces or missing APIs, immediate machine-observable evidence of success, tolerable failure consequences, and clear escalation routes.
insights.speaker: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
insights.so_what: A ready-made seven-point screen for sizing which of a company's processes are automatable now versus later.
insights.quote: they are best suited for tasks with immediate, machine-observable evidence of success, tolerable failure consequences, and clear escalation routes
insights.locator: Enterprises can and are benefiting from computer-using agents

source_meta.author: Fabrizio Serafini, Seema Amble, Eric Zhou
